name: Arts and Crafts art pottery
summary: Hand-made British art pottery after 1872. The potters of Lambeth, Chelsea and Fulham used salt glaze and ruby lustre, and made each piece one by one with a visible hand.

philosophy.core_thesis: A pot is a work of art when one person makes it from clay and glaze, and the hand is allowed to show.
design_principles: Make each piece by hand, with the maker's mark or initials incised in the base.
Throw or build the form with small irregularities of 1 to 3 mm; do not hide the throwing rings.
Fire a salt glaze at about 1200 °C and let it run to an orange-peel surface.
Fire a ruby or gold lustre in reduction at about 600 to 800 °C, so that the copper and silver show as a film.
Paint or incise plants, birds, fish and fantastic creatures, in a free line after Persian and Iznik models.
Use a limited palette of 3 or 4 colours: blue, turquoise, brown and ruby.
Keep the form plain and the surface rich.
Place the pot at home as a decorative object, not as a service.
anti_patterns: Identical factory copies with a printed pattern
A thin, regular, white body with a clear glaze
A surface so smooth that no hand shows

form.shape: Vases, bottle vases, lidded jars, bowls and grotesque bird jars, in a full, simple shape.
form.profile: A round belly with a short or tall neck; some pieces have a lobed or fluted wall, and the grotesque jars have a head as a lid.
form.foot_and_rim: A plain, slightly irregular foot, often unglazed; the rim is rolled or flared, with a thick lip.
form.proportion: Height 15 to 40 cm; the wall is 4 to 10 mm, thick and heavy in the hand.
rules: Throw the main form on the wheel and add incised detail while the clay is soft.
Keep the foot and the base unglazed or lightly glazed.
Sign the piece with a cipher, a date and the name of the shop.

bodies.rule: Use a buff or grey stoneware for salt glaze and an earthenware for tile and lustre. Make the body coarse enough to show the hand.

methods: incising and carving in leather-hard clay
forming.joins: Handles, feet and heads are added while the clay is soft and blended by hand; the join stays visible.
forming.details: Visible throwing rings, a thumb mark under the handle, an incised monogram, and a glaze that gathers thick in the lower curves.

glaze.pattern: Fish, birds, flowers and Persian scrolls in ruby lustre or in blue and turquoise; incised bands of birds and animals on salt-glazed stoneware.
glaze.gloss: Satin to high gloss, 30 to 80 GU, with a variable surface; lustre gives a metallic sheen.
glaze.wear: Salt glaze keeps its orange-peel texture for a long time; lustre dulls where it is touched.

palette.strategy: Deep, earthy blues and greens with a ruby and gold lustre, on a pale or buff ground.

firing.kiln: A small coal or wood kiln; a special muffle or reduction kiln for lustre.
processes: painting of the lustre pigment on a glazed tile or pot
reduction lustre firing at 600 to 800 °C with smoke
firing.scale: One to a few thousand pieces a year from a small shop; each pot is different.
firing.signs: A visible hand, uneven glaze, orange-peel salt glaze, and a lustre that shifts colour in the light.

pieces.form: Large vase with a ruby lustre peacock and a bold neck
Bottle vase of grey stoneware with an incised band of birds
Grotesque bird jar with a head as a lid
Wide bowl with fish in blue and turquoise and an irregular rim
Tall baluster vase with scratched flowers through a coloured slip

positive: British Arts and Crafts art pottery

canonical_works.work: Ruby lustre charger with a peacock
Salt-glazed stoneware vase with incised birds

Bottle vase with birds, Martin Brothers, MET
Jug by Martin Brothers, 1890, Fitzwilliam Museum

emotion.target_response: A feeling of warmth and honest work: the viewer sees a hand-made pot with a rich glaze and feels the person who made it.

use_cases: a hand-made vase for an Arts and Crafts interior
a museum label on late Victorian art pottery
avoid_when: the brief needs precise identical forms
the brief needs thin white porcelain
the brief is for a modern minimal object

modifiers.how: Remove the lustre and the bright colour; use a high-fired stoneware with a brown or green ash glaze.
Change the form to a flowing curve and the glaze to a flambé or a crystal.
